The common marmoset Callithrix jacchus, a small-bodied New World primate inhabiting the northeastern forests of Brazil, exhibits a suite of life-history traits shaped by its cooperative breeding system and highly frugivorous-insectivorous diet. Neonates emerge weighing approximately 26.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 26.5 grams], a relatively substantial birth mass for a platyrrhine of its adult dimensions, requiring significant maternal investment during intrauterine development. Gestation in this species proceeds over a period of 144 days [tg = 144 days] at a core body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that reflects the energetic demands of twin pregnancies, which are extremely common in marmosets. The ultimate adult body length, measured from crown to rump, reaches about 13.5 centimeters [Li = about 13.5 centimeters], placing the species among the larger callitrichids. This compact body plan is accompanied by a relatively high surface-area-to-volume ratio that influences thermoregulatory costs, particularly given that average resting body temperatures hover near 36 °C.

Offspring remain entirely dependent on parental care throughout an extended period of postnatal development, with nutritional independence from milk achieved at roughly 62 days after birth [tx = roughly 62 days after birth] under the standard thermal conditions of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. By this weaning age, infant marmosets have increased their body mass substantially, attaining an average wet weight of 86.67 grams [Wwx = 86.67 grams], a nearly threefold increase from their birth weight that underscores the efficiency of biparental and alloparental provisioning. The transition from milk to solid foods is gradual, typically involving begging for insects and fruit pulp from older group members, who carry the young dorsally. This reliance on cooperative infant care is a defining behavioral feature of the species and reduces the energetic burden on the mother alone. After weaning, the suckling juvenile enters a prolonged phase of somatic growth that precedes reproductive maturation.

Reproductive maturity in the common marmoset is reached after a considerable juvenile and subadult period. When maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], females attain puberty at approximately 382 days after birth [tp = 382 days after birth], while males mature somewhat later at about 477 days after birth [tp = about 477 days after birth]. This sex-based difference in maturation timing is common among callitrichids and is thought to reflect the different physiological demands placed on males, who must establish competitive positions within the social hierarchy before breeding successfully. The delay in male puberty likely corresponds to the time required for testicular descent and the onset of spermatogenesis. Once attained, the reproductive lifespan of both sexes can be substantial, and captive colonies frequently maintain breeding pairs for many years. The species does not exhibit strict seasonal breeding, instead demonstrating a capacity for continuous reproduction in favorable environments.

The maximum recorded longevity for Callithrix jacchus maintained under controlled captive conditions, with ambient temperatures regulating metabolic demands at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], is approximately 22.8 years [am = approximately 22.8 years], translating to about 8322 days [am = about 8322 days] if calculated on a 365-day calendar. This remarkable lifespan for such a small primate is likely facilitated by the protective social environment and consistent food availability typical of managed colonies, in contrast to the elevated predation and resource uncertainty faced by wild conspecifics. Senescence in the common marmoset is characterized by progressive loss of muscle mass, dental wear, and reduced mobility, eventually culminating in natural death. Comparative data from wild populations suggest substantially shorter lifespans, often under a decade, emphasizing the strong influence of extrinsic mortality factors.

Mature adults ultimately reach a stable asymptotic body mass, with fully grown individuals attaining an ultimate wet weight of approximately 255.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 255.2 grams], a value that is somewhat dimorphic, with males tending slightly heavier in many captive populations. This adult mass supports a maximum reproductive output that is comparatively high among primates: females in optimal condition can produce up to 2 offspring per litter [N_R_i = up to 2 offspring per litter], with a frequency of approximately 2.3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.3 litters per year] when housed at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], giving a potential yearly output of around 4 to 5 infants under ideal husbandry conditions. This extraordinary reproductive rate, far exceeding that of most haplorhines, is made possible by twin-bearing, postpartum estrus, and the extensive alloparental care system that allows mothers to reduce interbirth intervals dramatically. The combination of rapid maturation, high fecundity, and extended longevity positions the common marmoset as a life-history outlier among primates of equivalent body size.
